record.paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
record.original_question: Can observations of solar flares, including X-ray and gamma-ray measurements and flare thermal, non-thermal, and magnetic parameters, be used to infer the properties and evolution of coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particles, and what is the physical relationship between particles accelerated in the flare and the solar energetic particles observed later?

evidence.quote: • Can CME and Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) properties be inferred from ﬂare observations (including X-ray and γ-rays), which ﬂare parameters (thermal, non-thermal, magnetic) best constrain their evolution [32], and how are ﬂare accelerated particles and SEPs related?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A solar flare is a sudden release of magnetic energy in the solar corona that produces electromagnetic radiation across the spectrum, including hard X-ray and gamma-ray emission generated by accelerated electrons and ions interacting with the ambient plasma. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a large-scale eruption of magnetized plasma from the Sun's atmosphere into the heliosphere. Solar energetic particles (SEPs) are protons, electrons, and heavier ions accelerated to high energies, observed in situ near 1 AU, with sources commonly attributed both to flare reconnection sites and to CME-driven shocks.

For each flare event, define an observation vector consisting of:
(i) thermal flare parameters: peak emission measure, peak electron temperature, and their time evolution inferred from soft X-ray spectra;
(ii) non-thermal flare parameters: hard X-ray and gamma-ray photon spectra and their time evolution, including spectral index, low- and high-energy cutoffs, and inferred accelerated-electron and accelerated-ion energy content;
(iii) magnetic flare parameters: photospheric and coronal magnetic field measurements characterizing the active region, reconnection flux, and free magnetic energy.

For each associated CME, define an outcome vector consisting of its kinematic and morphological properties (mass, speed, acceleration, width, direction). For each associated SEP event, define an outcome vector consisting of peak intensity, spectral indices, elemental and isotopic composition, charge states, and onset/release times of protons, electrons, and ions at 1 AU.

Address the following questions:

1. Determine whether there exists a deterministic or statistical mapping from the flare observation vector to the CME outcome vector and the SEP outcome vector that constrains these outcomes more tightly than climatological priors, and identify which subset of thermal, non-thermal, and magnetic flare parameters yields the strongest constraint on CME and SEP evolution.

2. Characterize the physical relationship between the population of particles accelerated in the flare itself (as inferred from X-ray and gamma-ray emission) and the SEP population observed later in interplanetary space, including the extent to which the latter is composed of, reaccelerated from, or independent of the former, and quantify how this relationship depends on flare and CME properties.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a recognized open question in solar and heliospheric physics. The connection between flare-accelerated particles and SEPs, and the predictability of CME/SEP properties from flare observations, remains an active area of investigation with no consensus answer; recent reviews and decadal-survey-style documents continue to frame these as outstanding problems.

status_evidence.title: Solar Energetic Particles: Acceleration and Transport (review)
status_evidence.snippet: The relative contributions of flare and CME-shock acceleration to observed SEP events remain debated.
status_evidence.claim: The flare-vs-shock origin of SEPs is still an open question.

status_evidence.title: Connecting flare X-ray/gamma-ray observations to SEPs
status_evidence.snippet: Studies continue to investigate whether flare hard X-ray and gamma-ray signatures can predict SEP properties, with mixed correlations.
status_evidence.claim: Inference of SEP properties from flare observations is partially correlated but not deterministically established.
